newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MMS disputes agency watchdog royalty attack.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MMS disputes agency watchdog royalty attack.

text.p: The U.S. Minerals Management Service defended its settlements of oil, gas and minerals royalty disputes in face of criticism that it might have collected far less than it was owed, the Interior Department's watchdog said in a report released Thursday.
The agency garnered $218 million in the 10 negotiated settlements reviewed by the inspector general, but the total was $94 million less than it first estimated was due.
The report slammed MMS for leaving out crucial information, which made it impossible for the watchdog to assess whether the agency had settled for too little.
But the agency said the report did not necessarily fault the settlements themselves.
"Change in the amount between (the preliminary) audit and settlement, doesn't necessarily mean the money owed has been compromised," said MMS spokesman Tom DeRocco.
The inspector general reviewed ten deals out of 97 totaling $320 million negotiated between April 1993 and March 1995.
Most of the cases involved disputes on royalties owed for oil and natural gas production on federal lands.

"Specifically, for 9 of the 10 settlements reviewed, there was no documentation for the estimated values of the issues concerning the underpayment of royalties to be negotiated, the arguments for reducing values of issues, and/or the reasons why the values of issues were reduced as a result of negotiations," the report said.

Commenting on a recommendation that the agency should do more work to estimate the value of royalties owed ahead of negotiations, MMS said it "'does not believe that the increased complexity recommended is beneficial,'" according to agency remarks quoted in the report.
MMS balked at including more in its documents, fearing it would reveal its strategy and jeopardize future negotiations.
"There is still some concern that producing the level of documentation the (inspector general) wants ... could damage this alternative dispute resolution process," said DeRocco.

But the inspector general's report said that was no excuse. "Before a court orders the release of these documents, the court will have to make a determination that the release will not harm the Service in future negotiations," it said.
The agency has until December 6 to file a response to the final report.
The final report closely matched a draft version written by the inspector general last year and released in August by a government watchdog group, Project on Government Oversight.

MMS has come under pressure from lawmakers over the last year to be more aggressive in chasing after royalties. The agency annually collects about $4 billion from production on federal lands on- and offshore.
